units.name: Spy

tier.basis: Trained at the Allied barracks only once the side has a Radar Dome; the wiki infobox gives tier 2 and StrategyWiki the same two buildings. A Soviet side can train it in skirmish only from a captured Allied barracks, and the Soviet-owned Spy of the campaign is campaign-only, so the entry is recorded under the Allies.

cost_band.basis: Five times a Rifle Infantry's price and a little over half the main-battle-tank anchor, so low.

mobility.notes: Both wikis give it the same land speed as the Rifle Infantry, the speed reference.

body.notes: One soldier. Every player but its owner sees it drawn as a Rifle Infantry in that player's own colours (see abilities/0).

armour.notes: Half the Rifle Infantry's health. Step 1 of the armour-class order decided: the wiki infobox leaves the armour type as N/A and StrategyWiki gives none, which the armour map makes unarmoured; the manual's own Armor grade is None as well.

sensors.notes: Sees a quarter further than the Rifle Infantry, so medium. The disguise is a pattern, not the stealth trait: the spy is in plain view, only mistaken for a friendly rifleman. Inside an enemy Radar Dome it shares that enemy's view with its own side (abilities/1).

abilities.name: Disguise
abilities.summary: Always on. To every player but its owner the spy looks like one of that viewer's own Rifle Infantry, in the viewer's colours and under the rifleman's name, and this fools players allied with its owner too. Enemy units and base defences never pick it as a target by themselves, so it can stroll through a base unless a watchful human notices the stray rifleman and orders an attack, or an attack dog sees through it. Vehicles can still run it over.

abilities.name: Infiltrate
abilities.summary: Sent into an enemy building, the spy slips inside and is used up; the building keeps working. What its side learns depends on the building. Construction Yard, barracks, War Factory or Naval Yard: selecting it shows what it is building. Helipad and Airfield: that, plus the ammunition left in aircraft parked there. Power plants: a gauge of the enemy's power. Ore Refinery or Silo: how full it is (exact figures in the Remastered Collection). Radar Dome: the spy's side sees whatever that enemy sees. A fake building is shown up as a fake. A Sub Pen also earns a Sonar Pulse and an Airfield a parabomb strike (abilities/2 and abilities/3). Spies trained by a Soviet player show exact power and ore figures.

abilities.name: Sonar Pulse (earned in a Sub Pen)
abilities.summary: A spy that gets into an enemy Sub Pen puts a Sonar Pulse button on its side's sidebar. Used once, it briefly exposes every enemy submarine anywhere on the battlefield, so ships can find and hit them; then it is gone. In multiplayer the code grants it only when superweapons are switched on. In the Remastered Collection it keeps recharging while the infiltrated Sub Pen stands (patch 740600).

abilities.name: Parabombs (earned in an Airfield)
abilities.summary: A spy that gets into an enemy Airfield gives its side one parabomb strike. The player picks a spot; a Badger bomber flies over and lets a row of bombs on parachutes drift down, wrecking the target and what stands near it, while soldiers who see them falling try to run clear. It works once. In multiplayer the code grants it only when superweapons are switched on; otherwise parabombs are a Soviet power of the campaign only.

strengths.why: Enemy units and base defences never choose it as a target on their own, so it can walk through a base that keeps no dogs.
One spy in an enemy Radar Dome gives its side the enemy's view; others expose production, power, stored ore or fake buildings.
Inside an enemy Airfield it earns a free parabomb strike that wrecks a target and its surroundings.
Inside an enemy Sub Pen it earns a pulse that shows every enemy submarine for a few seconds.

weaknesses.why: Half a rifleman's health and no weapon of any kind, so it dies at once to whoever does decide to shoot it.
It fools the game's targeting, not people: a careful human player spots a rifleman where none should be and has it shot.
Each spy is spent on a single building, and most buildings give only information.

countered_by.why: Attack dogs see through the disguise and hunt spies down by themselves; computer opponents rely on them to stop spies.
Attack dogs see through the disguise and hunt spies down by themselves; computer opponents rely on them to stop spies.
Like any soldier it can be run over, and computer-driven vehicles sometimes flatten an enemy spy without meaning to.

counters.why: Sent into an enemy building, it lays bare what the building does: a Radar Dome shares the enemy's view, factories show what they are building, power plants and refineries give away power and stored ore, and a fake building is shown up.
The Sonar Pulse it earns briefly exposes every enemy submarine, wherever it lurks, so ships can hunt them.
The Sonar Pulse it earns briefly exposes every enemy submarine, wherever it lurks, so ships can hunt them.

units.memorable: Everyone who looks at it sees one of their own riflemen; only a dog can tell, and one spy in the right building hands over the enemy's view, sonar or a bomber strike.
units.as_player: You look like a rifleman of whoever is watching, so bots and turrets ignore you, but sharp players notice a soldier in the wrong place. Walk into an enemy building to spend your life on its secret: share their view, learn what they build, or earn a one-time sonar ping or bomber strike for your team. Unarmed and fragile: one dog, or one player who calls you out, ends the run.

Scout rests on the infiltrate button (the Radar Dome's shared view) and on the earned Sonar Pulse. The wiki's own prose calls spies great scouts, but no official text uses the scout label or an alias, so it ranks at step 2.

The building-by-building effects come from the Spy page's table. The manual also says a spy can show how many units the enemy has, which the table does not list, and a Supply depot is listed with no effect. The code (INFANTRY.CPP) does not say how long the shared Radar Dome view lasts.

The Parabombs page's infobox describes the campaign power (Soviet, with a long recharge); the one-time strike a spy earns comes from that page's prose and from INFANTRY.CPP, which enables it as a one-time power.

units.name: Attack Dog

tier.basis: Trained only at the Kennel, a Soviet building that needs nothing but the barracks; the wiki lists both the dog and the Kennel at tier 1.

cost_band.basis: Twice a Rifle Infantry's price and under a quarter of the main-battle-tank anchor: among the cheapest units.

mobility.notes: Both wikis give it the Rifle Infantry's land speed. By EA's code it walks at the rifleman's pace on a plain move order and charges at nearly twice it whenever it has a target; the band counts the charge, the way it moves in a fight (see uncertain).

body.notes: A German shepherd; the size list names war dogs as small.

armour.notes: About a quarter of the Rifle Infantry's health. Step 1 of the armour-class order decided: the wiki infobox gives N/A and StrategyWiki none, which the armour map makes unarmoured; the manual also calls dogs unarmoured. Unlike other soldiers, dogs never drop prone, so they never get the prone soldier's halved damage.

sensors.notes: Sees a quarter further than the Rifle Infantry. Detector: the manual makes it the only unit that can see through the Spy's disguise, and it attacks spies in reach on its own. No source says it unmasks a spy for teammates.

armament.name: Dog bite (the manual's Sharp teeth)
armament.summary: Runs at a soldier, springs at him from about three quarters of a rifle's reach and mauls him. The bite kills any soldier outright, whatever his health, and hurts nobody else nearby. It can be aimed only at infantry: never at a vehicle, building, aircraft, ship or patch of ground. Only one dog may go for a given soldier at a time, so any other dog must pick another victim. Victims never shoot back at a dog by reflex; it must be picked as an ordinary target.

strengths.why: One bite kills any soldier outright, whatever his health, so even the toughest infantry fall to it.
The only unit that sees through spies, and it goes after them on its own.
Cheap and early: twice a rifleman's price, from a Kennel that needs only the barracks.

weaknesses.why: About a quarter of a rifleman's health, so a single rifle burst kills it.
The bite works only on soldiers: no vehicle, building, aircraft, ship or patch of ground, and only one dog may take a given soldier at a time.
It must run up and spring, so it is under fire all the way in.

countered_by.why: Rifle infantry kill a dog with one burst, and a group of them standing still is the worst thing to send dogs at.
Rifle infantry kill a dog with one burst, and a group of them standing still is the worst thing to send dogs at.
Nothing it does can harm a vehicle, so armour ignores it.

counters.why: A base guard that sees through spies and catches thieves, killing either with one bite.
The only unit that can find a spy, and it kills one with one bite.
A cheap base guard against engineers slipping in to take buildings.
Flamethrower troops struggle to hit a charging dog with their slow shots.
Grenadiers' slow grenades struggle to catch a charging dog.

units.memorable: A cheap, frail dog that kills any soldier in one leap, can't touch a tank, and no other unit in the game can sniff out a spy.
units.as_player: Cheap and quick to buy: sprint at a soldier and spring on him to kill him outright, however tough he is, but you can't bite vehicles or buildings, and only one dog may maul a target at a time. You sniff out disguised spies for your side. A single rifle burst ends you, so strike the isolated and the slow.

sources.note: Infobox: tier 1, needs the Soviet barracks; trains only attack dogs, and more Kennels train them faster.

uncertain.note: The infobox reach is about three quarters of the Rifle Infantry's rifle, which would be medium by the figure. The band is melee because the dog covers that gap by its own leap and bites on contact (INFANTRY.CPP takes it off the map during the leap and puts it back on the hit), and the melee band counts a unit's own leap.
Melee, as a lunge that lands at touching distance. Ram was the other reading, since the dog itself flies at the target, but it survives the hit and mauls rather than collides.

The sources only say the dog itself sees through spies and attacks them, and the code still draws a spy as a friendly rifleman to everyone else; the detector's coding rule covers a unit that sees through them only itself. The Kennel page's production list also says dogs detect Thieves; no other page read says so.

The game code doubles the dog's stride whenever it has a target, with no meter, stamina or cooldown, so in a fight it runs at a little under twice the Rifle Infantry's pace, and the band counts that charge (EA's released code, INFANTRY.CPP). On a plain move order with no target it walks exactly at the rifleman's pace, which would be medium. The band rests on reading the charge as the way it moves in a fight.

Scout rests on the detector trait (step 4). The fast band also meets scout's requires, but by the raider or scout tie-break speed alone makes a scout only when official text calls the unit one, and the Kennel page's production list, which calls the dog scout infantry, is the wiki's own words. Raider enters at step 4 too, through the fast band with no armour, and comes after scout in the roles list. Its description fits only loosely: the dog page warns against sending dogs at groups of riflemen and calls rocket soldiers and unarmed infantry easy prey, which comes close to picking off isolated targets, but no source has the dog pull back after a kill, and the manual presents it as a base guard. With a medium band (see mobility/speed), raider would drop out.
Rests on the dog page's own prose, which says grenadiers and flamethrowers defend poorly against dogs because their shots travel slowly.
Rests on the same prose as counters/3.

units.name: Field Mechanic

tier.basis: Trained at the Allied Barracks only once a Service Depot stands: its infobox gives tier 2 with that requirement, and the depot's page lists him among the units it unlocks. The registry counts the depot as one tech step beyond the basics.

cost_band.basis: List price a little above the Medium Tank's and just past the medium threshold, a high price for a soldier, as the wiki remarks.

mobility.notes: His land speed in the infobox equals the Rifle Infantry's, so medium. The Aftermath manual calls him slow, a word about him among soldiers that does not set the band. The vehicles he serves outpace him: the Medium Tank moves nearly twice as fast. Like any soldier he can be run over by a crushing vehicle.

body.notes: An ordinary soldier carrying a socket wrench; one per purchase.

armour.notes: Step 1 decided: the armour type none in the reference copy of the Aftermath rules file maps to unarmoured, and the Aftermath manual also grades him as wearing no armour; the wiki's infobox says Light (see uncertain). He has a little more health than a Rifle Infantry and less than a Medic. Like other infantry he drops flat when frightened and then takes half damage, a game-wide rule that adds no model.

sensors.notes: The infobox sight is three quarters of the Rifle Infantry's, inside medium but close to the short edge. No sensor trait of his own; the engine lets every soldier make a cloaked enemy beside it shimmer into view, which is game-wide.

armament.name: Socket Wrench
armament.summary: Restores health to a damaged friendly vehicle and can never be turned on an enemy. Ordered onto a hurt vehicle, or left idle near one, he walks over and works on it until it is whole, which takes a while, as with the Medic's healing. The wiki says this is far quicker than a trip to the Service Depot and costs nothing, whereas the depot bills credits for each repair and the vehicle must drive back onto its pad. The code also accepts friendly aircraft as patients, but never ships or soldiers. A board order on a damaged transport becomes a repair order: he fixes it fully first and only then climbs in.

crew.notes: One soldier. He rides in an APC like any infantry (entering is a universal key), but only once the carrier is at full health, because his repair order takes over while it is damaged (wiki; INFANTRY.CPP). In the 2020 source release a force move sends him into a damaged APC without the repair.

on_death.notes: No page shows anything special when he dies; the code has no survivor logic for infantry.

strengths.why: Mends friendly vehicles where they fight, for free and, by the wiki's account, far quicker than a Service Depot, so tanks need not leave the front to be fixed.
Finds damaged friendly vehicles near him by himself and keeps at them until they are fully repaired.

weaknesses.why: His one tool only repairs: he has no gun, so he can neither defend himself nor hurt anything.
A frail soldier the manual calls unarmoured; Soviet infantry and tanks pick him off easily, and crushing tanks can drive over him.
Walks at a rifleman's pace, which the manual calls slow, so the faster tanks he serves leave him behind.
Needs a Service Depot first and costs a little more than a Medium Tank, a steep price for a soldier who cannot fight.

countered_by.why: The manual singles out Soviet infantry as a threat to him; with no weapon he can only run from riflemen.
The manual also names Soviet tanks: their guns kill him quickly, and he cannot answer them.

combos.why: Follows friendly tanks and patches them up between engagements, so an armoured push keeps going without trips home.
An APC can carry him to the front under armour, but a damaged carrier must be fully repaired by him before he can climb in.

units.memorable: The Aftermath's wrench-carrying soldier who fixes friendly tanks in the field for free, quicker than the Service Depot, yet cannot fire a single shot.
units.as_player: A T2 Allied support pick with no gun. Follow your team's tanks and keep the wrench on damaged vehicles to bring them back to full for free. With little health and a rifleman's pace, stay behind the armour: enemy infantry and tanks will hunt you first.

So each repair lands the moment it is made: hitscan, a delivery the repair-tool family does not list (see atypical).

The reach comes from the reference copy of the Aftermath rules file (aftrmath.ini, OpenRA's raclassic repository): a little under two thirds of the Rifle Infantry rifle's, the registry's range reference, so short. The manual's grade Short agrees, though the registry notes say the manual's grades are not band data.

INFANTRY.CPP and TECHNO.CPP also accept friendly aircraft as patients, but TECHNO.CPP fires at an aircraft off the ground only a projectile with the anti-aircraft flag, and the reference copy of the Aftermath rules file gives the wrench the invisible projectile, which lacks it. So he can treat a flier only while it stands on the ground, which is not an air target, and only ground vehicles are listed.

That he is faster than the depot and free is the wiki's own prose; the manual says only that he takes time to bring a vehicle back to full strength. The reference copy of the Aftermath rules file gives his rate: each use of the wrench restores about a quarter of a main battle tank's health, then he waits a few seconds before the next. No page sets that against the depot's pace.

The force-move exception for a damaged APC is in the 2020 source release; whether the 1997 to 1999 game already had it is unchecked. The wiki describes only the rule that he repairs the carrier first.

atypical.note: The reference copy of the Aftermath rules file and EA's released BULLET.CPP show the wrench's repair landing on the vehicle the moment it is used, from a short way off and with no flight; the repair-tool family lists only beam and projectile deliveries.

units.name: M.A.D. Tank

tier.basis: Built at the Soviet War Factory once a Soviet Tech Center stands; its infobox gives tier 3, and the wiki's War Factory list files it under tier 3 as a unit of The Aftermath only. It counts as buildable in skirmish and in Aftermath-mode multiplayer, as the registry's version note says. A side that holds a captured Soviet War Factory together with the buildings it needs can also build it (War factory (Red Alert 1) page).

cost_band.basis: List price about two and a half times the main-battle-tank anchor, well past the very-high threshold, for a unit that is used up in a single blast. The Russian country discount is ignored.

mobility.notes: Built on the Mammoth Tank's chassis. Its land speed is about seven tenths of the Rifle Infantry's pace and three quarters of the Mammoth's, and well under half the Medium Tank's, so it is slower than both. It rolls over infantry (wiki; the crusher flag in the game code). Once its countdown starts it never moves again. Like every damaged vehicle it slows down at half health or less (game-wide), which the band ignores.

body.notes: The wiki says it uses the Mammoth Tank's chassis and carries a large piston on its back that pumps faster as the charge builds; the code gives it no turret. Launcher-rack is the nearest body plan (an exposed device on a chassis with no passenger room), although the chassis is a heavy one, not a light one (see fit_notes). Coded large: it is a tank, and the code's sprite-size flag groups it with the Medium, Heavy and Mammoth Tanks.

armour.notes: Step 1 decided: the infobox armour type Heavy maps to heavy, and the RA1 registry notes step the M.A.D. Tank down to medium as a ground vehicle with less health than the main battle tanks. It has half the health of the Mammoth Tank whose chassis it uses, and the wiki stresses that it is far easier to destroy. The manual's Armor word (heavy) is a grade, not the class. The Soviet Iron Curtain, a side-wide power, can make it immune to damage for a while, which also holds back its countdown.

sensors.notes: Its sight is half again the Rifle Infantry's, exactly on the edge, which goes to medium; the Mammoth sees as far. No sensor trait. Its pulse reaches well past what it can see.

crew.notes: One player drives and starts the countdown. In the source a single crewman climbs out when the countdown begins and runs off (wiki); the code makes him a civilian technician armed only with a feeble pistol.

abilities.name: Harmonic shock wave (activate)
abilities.summary: Clicking the selected tank on itself (in the Remastered Collection the Deploy key works too) sounds a siren and starts the charge. From then on the tank stays put and takes no more orders, and its lone crewman climbs out and runs. A piston on its back pumps faster and faster until the seismic pulse goes off and wrecks the tank itself. The charge cannot be called off: only destroying the tank first stops it, and then no pulse comes at all. While the Soviet Iron Curtain covers the tank, the charge cannot finish, which the wiki notes a rival Soviet player can use to stall it. The pulse reaches about three times as far as the tank can see. Every vehicle, ship and aircraft inside it, aircraft in flight included, loses a little under half of its own maximum health, and every building about two fifths, whichever side owns it and whatever its armour. Soldiers take no damage at all.

on_death.notes: The crewman gets out when the countdown starts, not at the moment of death; the tank then dies in its own pulse, which spares him. If enemies destroy the tank first, nothing explodes. The game code gives a vehicle without passenger seats that the rules mark as crewed an even chance of leaving a crewman when it is destroyed, but the reference copy of the Aftermath rules file marks this tank as not crewed, so an ordinary death leaves no one behind.

strengths.why: One pulse strips a little under half of the maximum health from every vehicle, ship and aircraft in a very wide area, flying aircraft too, and a large share from every building; armour makes no difference, so the wiki notes that three pulses finish off anything that is not infantry.
It runs over soldiers in its path, which the wiki says makes it dangerous to infantry even though its pulse leaves them unhurt.

weaknesses.why: Far less armour than the Mammoth it is built on, with half its health, so focused fire can kill it before the countdown ends, and then the pulse never comes.

Once started it cannot be stopped or moved, its pulse hurts its own side's vehicles and buildings as much as the enemy's, and it does nothing to infantry, so the wiki calls it almost useless for defence.
Slower than the Rifle Infantry and the Mammoth, so it is slow to reach its target and easy to see coming.
Needs a Soviet Tech Center and costs about two and a half main battle tanks, all spent in one blast.

countered_by.why: The pulse cannot hurt soldiers, so infantry can keep shooting it through the whole countdown; the wiki names infantry as its best counter.
Rocket weapons are made to hurt vehicles; the wiki names rocket infantry as the best counter.
Red Alert's own rocket infantry, the counter the wiki names: untouched by the pulse and armed against vehicles.

counters.why: Every vehicle in the pulse loses the same large share of its maximum health whatever its armour, so a massed tank column is gutted at once.
Damage by share of maximum health makes thick armour worthless: the toughest tanks lose as large a share as the lightest trucks.
Buildings in range lose a large share of their health to each pulse, and three pulses level any building, so a few of these tanks can break a base.

combos.why: The wiki notes that three pulses in a row destroy any vehicle or building, provided the target gets no chance to repair in between.
Soldiers are its counter and the pulse spares them, so escorts that clear infantry keep it alive through the countdown.

units.memorable: A tank that is a countdown: once started, only its death stops the pulse that guts every vehicle and building around it, friend or foe, while soldiers walk away unhurt.
units.as_player: A slow, unarmed T3 tank that is one big bomb. Drive into the enemy and press the key: the tank locks in place behind a siren and a long, loud charge, and when it ends every vehicle and building nearby, your team's too, loses a big share of its health. You hop out as a soldier when the charge starts and slip away, since the pulse spares soldiers. That same rule makes enemy infantry your hunters during the countdown.

Active or deploy. The Remastered Collection patch 735514 page (Command & Conquer Wiki, read, not cited) says the Deploy key starts it, and the tank never moves again once the charge starts, but it gains no mode: it only counts down to its own death. Coded active.

units.name: Mobile Gap Generator

tier.basis: Built at the Allied War Factory once an Allied Tech Center stands; its infobox gives tier 3. The manual marks it as a multiplayer-only unit (it adds that such units may turn up in some single-player missions), so players build it only in skirmish and multiplayer; StrategyWiki says the same. A side that holds a captured Allied War Factory together with the buildings it needs can also build it (War factory (Red Alert 1) page).

cost_band.basis: List price a little over two thirds of the main-battle-tank anchor, inside low; StrategyWiki gives the same multiplayer price.

mobility.notes: The wiki calls it a gap generator mounted on a truck, on wheels. By the rules file's figure, the one the game reads, it moves about two thirds faster than the Rifle Infantry and a little slower than the Medium Tank; the C&C Wiki's infobox figure would make it much slower (see uncertain). It runs over infantry (the crusher flag in the game code), though the crush trait is kept for large and huge units (see atypical). Like every damaged vehicle it slows down at half health or less (game-wide), which the band ignores.

body.notes: A truck carrying the gap generator; the code gives it a rotating dish and no gun turret, which fits launcher-rack's chassis with an exposed mast or sensor gear. Medium, as the size list puts trucks; the code's sprite-size flag, which groups it with the Medium and Heavy Tanks (drawn bigger than one cell), counts only for a unit that no example covers.

armour.notes: Step 1 decided: the infobox armour type Light maps to light, and StrategyWiki and the manual's grade agree. It has very little health.

sensors.notes: Its sight equals the Rifle Infantry's; StrategyWiki gives the same. No sensor trait: the gap field hides an area from the enemy, not just the truck, which neither stealth nor jammer describes (see fit_notes). The code does not make it a radar jammer, unlike the Radar Jammer truck, nor hide it from radar by itself.

crew.notes: One player drives; there is nothing to fire. The reference copy of the rules marks the truck as crewed, with a crewman who can get out (see on_death), but no page says how many ride in it.

abilities.name: Shroud generator (gap field)
abilities.summary: Always on, with no button. The truck keeps a small patch of ground around itself under black shroud for its enemies and keeps renewing it, so the field travels with it; the truck and any units close by drop out of the enemy's view. An enemy unit that drives in uncovers only the ground within its own sight, and the shroud settles over that ground again once it moves on or dies. The field is smaller than the one the Gap Generator building casts. Computer opponents ignore shroud altogether, so it only fools human players. Remastered Collection patch 744746 fixed a bug that left its shroud on the map for good.

on_death.notes: The reference copy of the rules marks the truck as crewed, and the game code gives such a vehicle without passenger seats an even chance, when it is destroyed, of letting one crewman out with part of his health; since it has no weapon, he is a civilian technician with only a feeble pistol. He gets out only by chance. The code also takes its field away when it is destroyed.

strengths.why: Its gap dish keeps the ground around it black for the enemy, hiding the truck and every unit near it, so the enemy cannot see what is being sent against them.
It can run over infantry, its only way of hurting anything.

weaknesses.why: Light armour and very little health, so it dies fast once found.
It carries the gap dish instead of a gun, so it cannot fight back.
Its field is smaller than the gap generator building's, so escorts must keep close, and the computer opponent, which ignores shroud, is not fooled by it, so it pays off only against human players.

countered_by.why: A scout that drives into the field uncovers the ground within its own sight and sees what hides there; the shroud only closes again after it leaves or is destroyed.
It has no gun and light armour, so any armed vehicle that finds it can destroy it unopposed.

counters.why: Scouts and lookouts watching from outside the field see only shroud, so they cannot read the size or make-up of the force under it.
Long-range guns that need others to spot for them find no targets under the field until their own units come close enough to uncover them.

combos.why: Driving with an attack group, it keeps the whole group under its field, so the enemy sees nothing of the push until it arrives; the wiki recalls enemy trucks hiding advancing attackers this way in a Soviet campaign mission.

units.memorable: A truck with no gun that fights with darkness: the ground around it and its escorts stays black for the enemy, who sees only what his own units stand next to.
units.as_player: An unarmed T3 support truck. You carry no gun: drive with your team and the ground around all of you stays dark for the enemy, so they cannot see what is coming. An enemy who drives in sees only what is next to him, and the dark closes again when he leaves. Light, fragile and with nothing to shoot back with, you die quickly once found, so stay inside your escort.

units.name: Minelayer

tier.basis: Built at the Allied War Factory once a Service Depot stands; the Anti-tank minelayer page's infobox gives tier 2 with that requirement, and the registry counts the depot as one tech step.

cost_band.basis: List price equal to the Medium Tank's and a little under the anchor (the other side's minelayer costs the same); exactly on the medium threshold, so medium.

mobility.notes: Land speed a little over twice the Rifle Infantry's, so fast: a little quicker than both main battle tanks, the Medium Tank and the Heavy Tank. The code marks it as a vehicle that crushes infantry, so it has the crush trait, though the trait is kept for large and huge units (see atypical). Tracks rest on the Anti-personnel minelayer page's mention of treads, for the one unit type both sides build; the Anti-tank page names no drive.

body.notes: The Allied build of the one minelayer unit type (internal name MNLY), which a Soviet side fields with anti-personnel mines instead (ra1.soviet.minelayer): an enclosed hull with no turret that turns, opens a rear hatch and drops a mine, reusing the APC's door routine in the code. It carries mines, not troops. The manual calls it the AT Mine Layer and the wiki the Anti-tank minelayer.

armour.notes: Step 1 decided: the Anti-tank page leaves the armour type blank, so, as the RA1 registry notes direct, the Anti-personnel page's Heavy is taken for the one internal type both share; it maps to heavy, and the registry notes step both minelayers down to medium, since they have a quarter of a main battle tank's health. The wiki calls it tough enough to soak some punishment.

sensors.notes: The infobox sight is a quarter more than the Rifle Infantry's, the same as the main battle tanks'. No sensor trait.

crew.notes: One player drives and drops the mines. The reference copy of the rules marks the minelayer as crewed, with a crewman who can get out (see on_death), but no page says how many ride in it.

abilities.name: Mine deployment
abilities.summary: Double-clicking the minelayer where it stands (the Remastered Deploy key does the same) makes it turn, open its hatch and leave one anti-tank mine in the cell under it; a cell that already holds a mine or a building's foundation slab is refused. It holds five, shown as pips, and gets all five back free by driving onto a Service Depot, which reloads it before any repair. The game gives every Allied country this mine: it badly hurts or kills the first enemy vehicle to drive over it, while soldiers cross it unharmed and never set it off. Friendly vehicles never set it off, and units of the laying side path around their own mines. Laid mines stay hidden from enemy players and cannot be targeted directly; force fire on the ground clears them.

on_death.notes: The reference copy of the rules marks the minelayer as crewed, and the cited game code gives such a vehicle without passenger seats an even chance, when it is destroyed, of letting one crewman out with part of his health: a civilian technician, since it is unarmed. He gets out only by chance.

strengths.why: Each mine is deadly to vehicles: by the manual, one mine destroys most units, so a few mines stop an attack short of the base.
Quicker than either side's main battle tank, so it can seed an approach or an enemy ore field and get away again.
The wiki calls it tough enough to soak some punishment while it works.

weaknesses.why: Only five mines; every refill means a drive back to a Service Depot.
Its anti-tank mines never react to soldiers, who walk over them unharmed, so an infantry attack goes straight through its minefield.

countered_by.why: It has no gun and mines never touch fliers, so aircraft attack it freely; the wiki adds that a Yak force-firing at the ground clears a minefield.
Ordered to force fire at a patch of ground, a Yak's strafing guns set off every mine there, which the wiki recommends for clearing minefields.
Soldiers walk over its anti-tank mines unharmed, so its minefields never stop them; it has no gun, and running them down under its treads is its only answer.

counters.why: One mine is enough to kill a V2 rocket launcher and leaves a Heavy Tank badly hurt, so a mined approach blunts a tank push.
Mines laid in an enemy ore field catch the harvesters that come to gather there.
The wiki suggests mining enemy ore fields to wreck or hurt the Ore Trucks working them.

units.memorable: A fast, unarmed mine truck whose anti-tank mines can badly hurt or destroy most vehicles with a single blast yet let soldiers walk over them unharmed.
units.as_player: A fast, unarmed T2 vehicle. Drive to a choke point or an enemy ore field, press the mine key to drop one of your five anti-tank mines under you, then race back to the Service Depot to reload. Your mines wreck vehicles but do nothing to soldiers, so with no gun you live on speed, armour and the minefields you leave behind.

crew.notes: One player drives and drops the mines. The reference copy of the rules marks the minelayer as crewed, with a crewman who can get out (see on_death), but no page says how many ride in it.

abilities.name: Mine deployment
abilities.summary: Double-clicking the minelayer where it stands (the Remastered Deploy key does the same) makes it turn, open its hatch and leave one anti-personnel mine in the cell under it; a cell that already holds a mine or a building's foundation slab is refused. It holds five, shown as pips, and gets all five back free by driving onto a Service Depot, which reloads it before any repair. The game gives every Soviet country this mine: its blast kills every soldier close by, while an enemy vehicle that drives over it sets it off but is barely scratched. Friendly vehicles never set it off, but any soldier stepping on it triggers it, so units of the laying side path around their own mines. Laid mines stay hidden from enemy players and cannot be targeted directly; force fire on the ground clears them.

on_death.notes: The reference copy of the rules marks the minelayer as crewed, and the cited game code gives such a vehicle without passenger seats an even chance, when it is destroyed, of letting one crewman out with part of his health: a civilian technician, since it is unarmed. He gets out only by chance.

strengths.why: Each mine is deadly to soldiers: by the manual, one blast can wipe out a whole group of infantry, so a few mines guard the paths troops take toward the base.
Quicker than either side's main battle tank, so it can seed the routes enemy troops use and get away again.
The wiki calls it tough enough to soak some punishment while it works.

weaknesses.why: Only five mines; every refill means a drive back to a Service Depot.
Its anti-personnel mines barely scratch vehicles, so tanks roll straight through its minefield.

countered_by.why: It has no gun and mines never touch fliers, so aircraft attack it freely; the wiki adds that a Yak force-firing at the ground clears a minefield.
A rival Soviet player's Yak, ordered to force fire at a patch of ground, sets off every mine there with its strafing guns, which the wiki recommends for clearing minefields.
Its anti-personnel mines only scratch vehicles, and it cannot shoot back at the tanks rolling through.

counters.why: One blast kills every soldier near it, so a single mine can wipe out a whole group.

units.memorable: A fast, unarmed mine truck whose anti-personnel mines can wipe out a whole squad in one blast yet barely scratch a tank.
units.as_player: A fast, unarmed T2 vehicle. Drive to the paths enemy troops take, press the mine key to drop one of your five anti-personnel mines under you, then race back to the Service Depot to reload. Your mines shred soldiers but barely scratch tanks, so with no gun you live on speed, armour and the minefields you leave behind.

units.name: Mammoth Tank

tier.basis: Built at the War Factory once a Soviet Tech Center stands (the wiki's infobox; StrategyWiki agrees), and the manual's Tech Center entry names it among the high-tech units that building allows. The Tech Center is the t3 gate, and the wiki lists the tank as tier 3. The Service Depot requirement and the Allied side in the infobox apply only to Counterstrike's ant missions, which are left out. A side that holds a captured Soviet War Factory together with the buildings the tank needs can also build it (War factory (Red Alert 1) page).

cost_band.basis: List price from the wiki's infobox (StrategyWiki agrees): a little under twice the anchor of the two main battle tanks, which lands in high, just short of the very-high threshold. The Russian country discount is ignored, as the registry says.

mobility.notes: By the registry's paces, worked out from the game code, it moves a little slower than the Rifle Infantry: half the Allied Medium Tank's pace and a little over half the Soviet Heavy Tank's, the two main battle tanks, and the wiki calls it the slowest vehicle, though by the infobox figures the Aftermath's M.A.D. Tank, built on its chassis, is slower still. It runs over infantry in its path (StrategyWiki; the game code marks it as a crusher), and Force Move sends it onto a soldier on purpose (manual). Pivot is the tracks default. Like every damaged vehicle it slows down at half health or less (game-wide), which the band ignores.

body.notes: A tracked hull under one large turret that carries both the twin cannons and the two missile packs: the game code sets both weapons' firing points along the turret's facing, so they turn together. The manual says no tank is bigger and calls it the largest land weapons platform, and the wiki's prose calls it a super-heavy tank. But the code's size flag puts it in one group with the Medium and Heavy Tanks (and the Ore Truck and MCV): vehicles drawn larger than one map cell but under two cells across. No page says it is twice a tank's size, so it is coded large, a tank among tanks.

armour.notes: Check A decided: step 1 maps the infobox armour type Heavy to heavy, but the RA1 registry notes make the Mammoth super-heavy, the game's top tank, set apart from its battle tanks. It has half again the health of the Soviet Heavy Tank and the Allied Medium Tank. Self-repair: once at half health or below it slowly mends itself, and the healing stops at half (infobox; the self-healing check in TECHNO.CPP). A full repair needs the Service Depot, which is game-wide. No source gives it facing armour, and no armour upgrade exists. Side-wide powers stay off: the Soviet Iron Curtain can make it immune to damage for a while.

sensors.notes: The infobox sight figure is exactly half again the Rifle Infantry's, on the upper edge of medium, so it goes to medium. It sees a little further than the Medium and Heavy Tanks. No sensor trait: it has no radar of its own and detects nothing hidden.

armament.name: Twin 120mm cannons
armament.summary: Two heavy guns on the turret fire a pair of armour-piercing shells, one barrel just after the other, then wait a long while before the next pair. The manual rates them the most powerful guns on land, the wiki says the one-two shot works well against armour, and StrategyWiki calls them anti-armour cannons. Because the second shell leaves a moment later, it misses a moving target more often. They fire only at ground targets, never at aircraft; by the rules file's damage table their shells do three quarters of their full damage to the wood armour it gives buildings and half to concrete, and they can break walls. They reach a little over one and a half times as far as the Rifle Infantry's rifle. For each target the game compares how much this warhead and the missiles' warhead do to its armour type and fires the better one, preferring a weapon already in range, so only one of the two fires at a time.

armament.name: Mammoth Tusk missiles
armament.summary: Two missile packs on the same turret launch a pair of high-explosive homing missiles at ground or air targets, then wait out a long reload. The manual says they make the tank good against infantry and aircraft, the wiki adds buildings, and both wikis say a soldier often dies to a single hit. They are the tank's only weapon that reaches aircraft, and the wiki names the slow reload as the reason massed air attacks can overwhelm it. They reach a bit further than the cannons, about two thirds again the rifle's range. The game uses them on every aircraft and on any ground target whose armour suffers more from their warhead.

crew.notes: No player seats in the source. One player drives and fires both weapons. Both sit on the one turret, and the game fires only one of them at a time, picked for each target, so decision 2A proposes no gunner seat.

on_death.notes: The reference copy of the rules marks the Mammoth as crewed, and the game code gives a crewed ground vehicle without passenger seats an even chance, when it is destroyed, of letting one rifleman out with part of his health; he gets out only by chance. Its death also shakes the screen, and its explosion animation is bigger than most vehicles' but does no damage.

strengths.why: The biggest tank in the game, with half again the health of the main battle tanks: the manual says it can both take and deal heavy punishment.
The manual rates its twin cannons the most powerful guns on land; the paired shells hit armour hard.
Unlike the main battle tanks it can fire back at aircraft: its missiles reach every flier.
The missiles often kill a soldier with one hit and also work well against buildings.
Mends itself without a trip to the Service Depot once it falls to half health or below.

weaknesses.why: Among the slowest vehicles: a little slower than a rifleman and about half the main battle tanks' pace (the wiki calls it the slowest, though the Aftermath's M.A.D. Tank on its chassis is slower), so it cannot chase, and faster tanks can hit it and pull back.
After each pair of missiles it waits out a long reload, which leaves it open to a concentrated air attack.
Its guns fire slowly, and the second shell of each pair is more likely to miss a target on the move.
Needs a Tech Center, costs nearly twice a main battle tank and takes a long time to build.
The healing is slow and never lifts it above half health, so heavy damage still needs a depot.

countered_by.why: One on one it outguns any tank, but at equal cost several cheaper basic tanks outnumber it and destroy it with relative ease, above all when they catch it alone with hit-and-run attacks it is too slow to answer.
The wiki names Allied Medium Tanks among the basic tanks that swarm and kill a lone Mammoth; they are far faster.
The wiki also names Allied Light Tanks among the cheap tanks that outnumber and kill it in hit-and-run attacks.
A concentrated air attack overwhelms it while its missiles reload, and its cannons cannot fire upward at all.

counters.why: Its missiles often kill a soldier in one hit and it crushes the rest; the manual calls it effective against infantry.
Aircraft that come at it a few at a time get shot down: the manual credits its missiles against air units, which the main battle tanks cannot reach.
StrategyWiki rates it strong against structures, and the wiki says its missiles also work well on buildings.
One against one it outguns any tank: the manual rates its twin cannons the most powerful guns on land, and StrategyWiki rates it strong against vehicles. Several cheaper tanks beat it (countered by).

combos.why: The wiki warns it is most at risk when caught alone, so faster escort tanks that keep raiders off it suit it.
Its missiles reload slowly, so extra anti-air cover helps against the massed air attacks the wiki warns about.

units.memorable: Red Alert's biggest tank: twin cannons for armour, missile packs for infantry, buildings and even aircraft, and it mends itself, but only back up to half health.
units.as_player: A slow, costly T3 fortress. Left mouse fires the twin cannons, a staggered pair of anti-armour shells; right mouse fires the missile pair, which hits soldiers, buildings and aircraft, then reloads for a long while. The big turret turns slowly, so quick tanks can circle you. Below half health you slowly patch yourself back up to half, no further, and you crush soldiers you drive over, but you cannot outrun fast tanks or a massed air strike, so hold the line with your team.

sources.note: The Mammoth's unit type (internal name 4TNK): a turreted vehicle that crushes infantry, the firing points of both weapons along the turret line, and the large-unit size flag it shares with the Medium and Heavy Tanks.

uncertain.note: Step 1 finds no role label in the manual paragraph. Step 4 reads only the main weapon: the manual's praise of the missiles counts at roles.secondary step 3, its words on the cannons (unmatched on land) name no kind of target, and the rules file's warhead table gives no bonus. Step 5 gives assault (slow, heavy armour).

Anti-armour (StrategyWiki heading the cannons as anti-armour cannons), anti-infantry and anti-air (the manual's missile line) all rank at step 3, and the roles list order keeps anti-armour and anti-infantry; anti-air is third. Anti-armour rests only on that guide heading, a label under roles.secondary; without it the list would be anti-infantry and anti-air.

Large. The wiki's prose calls it a super-heavy tank and the manual the biggest tank, but super-heavy is a weight word, not a size, and the code's size flag (explained in REDALERT/TYPE.H of the same source release, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/electronicarts/CnC_Remastered_Collection/master/REDALERT/TYPE.H) puts it in one class with the Medium and Heavy Tanks. No page compares its footprint with a tank's, or says it is twice a tank's size.

No page read says in words that it runs on tracks. Every source calls it a tank, and the manual lets only tracked or heavy units overrun infantry with Force Move; the reference copy of Rules.ini (OpenRA's raclassic repository) marks it tracked, the flag the code reads.

It has the Rifle Infantry's Speed, but EA's released code cuts a tracked vehicle's throttle on open ground while a walking soldier keeps full throttle. So it is slower than the rifleman on straight runs and only just slower on diagonals. Every way of measuring gives slow, so the band does not rest on the edge rule, but the margin on diagonals is thin.

StrategyWiki heads the cannons as anti-armour guns and gives their target as ground, and the C&C Wiki's infobox lists them only under ground attack, so can_target step 3 applies, which lists structures only when a source says the weapon damages buildings. The reference copy of Rules.ini (OpenRA's raclassic repository, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OpenRA/raclassic/master/ref/Rules.ini) does: it gives the cannons the AP warhead, whose damage table has them do three quarters of full damage to the wood armour it marks as buildings' and half to concrete, and whose flags let them break walls. So structures are listed. The coders had split here, and the reconcile left structures out while that table could not be read; the C&C Wiki credits only the missiles with working on buildings.

The infobox gives one reach for ground and a slightly longer one for air without naming the weapons; StrategyWiki gives the shorter reach to the cannons and the longer one to the missiles. Both come out long either way, and neither reaches past the tank's own sight.

Projectile. The reference copy of Rules.ini (OpenRA's raclassic repository) gives the shells a flight speed well below the top projectile speed, which counts as saying they travel; projectile is also the cannon family default. The wiki's remark that the second shell misses moving targets more often fits a shell in flight.

Guided missiles with lock-on delivery. The reference copy of Rules.ini (OpenRA's raclassic repository) fires them as its HeatSeeker projectile, which it describes as a small homing missile and gives a non-zero rate of turn, the key that the file says makes a projectile home; REDALERT/BULLET.CPP of EA's source release (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/electronicarts/CnC_Remastered_Collection/master/REDALERT/BULLET.CPP; read, not cited) turns such a projectile toward its target as it flies. In a commanded game a missile that homes in by itself is a guided missile with lock-on delivery and no homing trait. The same projectile may be fired at aircraft and at ground targets, so the attack order can pick any target on the list. No wiki page says the missiles steer; the manual calls them missile packs.
No magazine: the pair of missiles repeats at the normal rate of fire, which is the wait the wiki calls a reload.

The physical mount comes from the game code (TECHNO.CPP fires both weapons along the turret's facing; UDATA.CPP gives the unit a turret and places the secondary weapon along it), not from any page's words. Without the code, the guided-missiles family default free-aim would apply.

The wiki says the self-repair works only while the tank is not taking damage; the healing check in TECHNO.CPP adds health on a timer whenever it is at or below half, with no check for recent hits, so it may also heal under fire. Self-repair is coded either way.

The death facts in the notes come from the game code: UNIT.CPP (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/electronicarts/CnC_Remastered_Collection/master/REDALERT/UNIT.CPP) for the even chance of a crewman getting out of a crewed vehicle without passenger seats and the screen shake, and ADATA.CPP (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/electronicarts/CnC_Remastered_Collection/master/REDALERT/ADATA.CPP) for the death animation, which does no damage. The reference copy of the rules (Rules.ini and aftrmath.ini in OpenRA's raclassic repository, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OpenRA/raclassic/master/ref/Rules.ini) marks the Mammoth as crewed, so with UNIT.CPP it shows a crewman getting out by chance: bail-out, basis in-game. None of these pages is cited, as the entry already has five sources.

The comparisons with the main battle tanks rest on the Heavy tank (Red Alert 1) and Medium tank (Red Alert 1) pages of the Command & Conquer Wiki, read but not cited. Their infobox figures back health in armour/notes, sight in sensors/notes and the reasons in strengths/0, strengths/2 and weaknesses/0. For speed, their Speed values, which the rules file repeats, go through the registry's code-based paces, as mobility.notes now says.
The remark on building it from a captured Soviet War Factory rests on the War factory (Red Alert 1) page of the Command & Conquer Wiki, which is read but not cited; it changes no code.

Two weaknesses rest only on the C&C Wiki's own prose: massed basic tanks that strike and pull back, and the slow missile reload that leaves it open to concentrated aircraft. No official text speaks to them.

The Mammoth tank (Red Alert 1) page calls it the slowest vehicle, but the infobox on the M.A.D. tank page of the Command & Conquer Wiki (https://cnc.fandom.com/wiki/M.A.D._tank; read, not cited) gives that Aftermath tank three quarters of the Mammoth's land speed. The same correction is made in mobility.notes.

Both combos are reasoned, not named by a page: no page read pairs the tank with a teammate. They follow from the C&C Wiki's warnings that it is in most danger when caught alone and that massed aircraft can catch it during its slow missile reload.

units.name: Yak

tier.basis: Built only at the Airfield, and the Airfield itself needs a Radar Dome (Airfield infobox); the Yak's infobox gives tier 2. As the registry notes ask for planes, the gate recorded is the Radar Dome, the tech step behind the Airfield. Its Allied version is campaign-only.

cost_band.basis: The list price sits exactly on the medium threshold, which takes the higher band: the same price as the Allied Medium Tank and a little under the main-battle-tank anchor.

mobility.notes: Its air speed is a little over four times the Rifle Infantry's pace. Among the game's aircraft it matches the Longbow, is a third quicker than the Hind and reaches four fifths of the MiG's speed; the manual still calls it not that fast. A fixed-wing plane that cannot hover or set down on open ground, only on its Airfield, and that must swing round to face its target before it fires, so it attacks in passes; its handling is the jet default.

body.notes: A single attack plane; its sprite and cameo follow the Second World War Yak-3 or Yak-9 fighter. Planes are large by the size examples (jets).

armour.notes: Step 1 decided: the infobox armour type Light maps to light. Its health is a little above the MiG's and about a quarter of the Hind's or the Longbow's. Like every aircraft it takes half damage while it is in the air (game-wide). Side-wide powers stay off: the Iron Curtain can make it immune for a while.

sensors.notes: The infobox gives it no sight range at all, as for every RA1 aircraft: in flight it clears no shroud and works from what its team already sees, and once landed it reveals only its own cell (game-wide). Planes in flight never show on the enemy's radar map (the Airfield's production list); that is game-wide and not the stealth trait.

armament.name: Twin machine guns
armament.summary: Two guns fire together in strafing passes. It fires only when its nose points almost straight at the target, and each burst is aimed at a point straight ahead along its heading, well inside its full reach, so the fire follows the plane's line of flight. The manual says one pass can wipe out a group of soldiers on the march. Small-arms warhead; ground and sea targets only, and the wiki has Yaks raiding outlying buildings too. Force-firing a patch of ground sets off the mines there. It carries 15 bursts, then flies home to reload. Reach is a bit over one and a half times the rifle's; it bands off-screen only because aircraft have no sight range of their own.

crew.notes: One pilot flies and fires. The source has no seats; the reference copy of the rules marks the plane as crewed, with a crewman who can get out (see on_death).

on_death.notes: The reference copy of the rules marks the Yak as crewed, and the game code drops a rifleman by parachute from a crewed aircraft nine times in ten when it goes down over ground a soldier can stand on; he gets out only by chance. If its Airfield is destroyed while it is airborne, the plane crashes (manual).

strengths.why: The manual nicknames it the infantry eraser: a single strafing pass can kill a whole group of marching soldiers.
It flies high, so only anti-air weapons such as Rocket Soldiers, AA guns and SAM sites can shoot at it.
Flying above minefields, it can force-fire on mined ground and clear the mines from the air, which the wiki rates it very good at.

weaknesses.why: After 15 bursts it must fly back to its Airfield, and a plane with that many rounds reloads far more slowly than the MiG or the Longbow.
It can land only on its own Airfield, one plane per Airfield, and it crashes if that Airfield is destroyed while it is in the air (manual).

Light armour and little health, and slower than the MiG, so it stays in reach: the wiki warns it will not last long against an AA gun that is still firing, and the manual says Rocket Soldiers who live through its first pass make easy prey of it.

countered_by.why: The wiki says to knock out SAM sites, AA guns and Rocket Soldiers before Yaks go in; the manual says AA guns badly damage any plane that flies over them.
The manual names Rocket Soldiers who survive the first strafing run as the Yak's natural killers.

counters.why: Its strafing passes cut down whole groups of soldiers (manual); StrategyWiki also rates it strong against infantry.
Minefields do not stop it: a force-fire order on the mined ground destroys the mines from the air (wiki).
Only Minelayers lay mines, so the minefields the wiki says it clears from the air are the Allied Minelayer's anti-tank fields.
A rival Soviet player's Minelayer lays anti-personnel fields instead, and a force-fire order clears those the same way.

combos.why: The wiki suggests heavy tanks as a distraction: they keep the defenders busy while Yaks hit the outlying buildings, once the AA guns are gone.
The Heavy Tank is the decoy the wiki names for Yak raids on a base.

units.memorable: The manual's infantry eraser: a Soviet attack plane that mows down marching soldiers in strafing passes, then must fly home to reload its many bursts.
units.as_player: A plane that never stops: you fly wide loops and line up passes, aiming the twin guns by pointing the nose down a line of soldiers. After 15 bursts you head back to your airfield pad for a slow reload. Only anti-air can touch you, so find the rocket troops and AA guns first, and force-fire into a minefield to open it for your tanks.

sources.note: The fixed-wing attack routine: a plane fires only when nearly facing its target, aims each burst at a point ahead along its heading and fires twice when it has two guns; an idle plane heads back to its landing building; airborne aircraft take half damage; and a crewed aircraft that is shot down drops a rifleman by parachute nine times in ten over ground a soldier can stand on.

uncertain.note: The comparisons with other aircraft (speed here, health in armour.notes) come from the infoboxes of MiG (Red Alert 1), Hind and Longbow (Red Alert 1) on the Command & Conquer Wiki, read but not cited. REDALERT/AADATA.CPP of the same source release (read, not cited) marks the Yak as fixed-wing, unable to land on clear ground and hidden on radar.

Structures rest on the Yak page's tip that Yaks can hit a base's outlying buildings, read with StrategyWiki's target line Ground; the reference copy of Rules.ini (OpenRA's raclassic repository, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OpenRA/raclassic/master/ref/Rules.ini) has its small-arms warhead do half its full damage to the wood armour it gives buildings and a quarter to concrete. Air is left out: the infobox's air attack line is empty, StrategyWiki says ground, and the copy gives the guns the invisible projectile without the anti-aircraft flag, which REDALERT/TECHNO.CPP of EA's source release (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/electronicarts/CnC_Remastered_Collection/master/REDALERT/TECHNO.CPP; read, not cited) requires for firing at an aircraft in the air.
Off-screen follows from aircraft having no sight range at all, as the registry notes expect; by reach alone the gun is long, and the manual grades its Range as Short, a grade the bands do not read.

Raider rests on the very fast band (a little over four times the rifleman's pace) with light armour. The manual calls the Yak not that fast, which is about it among aircraft; speed names no target, so the drop rule does not remove raider.
The Yak page's prose calls it less armoured than the MiG, but both infoboxes give armour type Light and the Yak slightly more health. The class is light either way; the infobox is followed.

Each Airfield holds one plane (manual), so the number of Yaks and MiGs together is tied to the number of Airfields built. That is a slot rule shared by both plane types and lifted by building more Airfields, not a fixed cap on the Yak, so it is coded open.

Bail-out, basis in-game: the reference copy of Rules.ini (OpenRA's raclassic repository, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OpenRA/raclassic/master/ref/Rules.ini) marks the Yak as crewed, and the cited AIRCRAFT.CPP parachutes a rifleman from a crewed aircraft that is shot down, nine times in ten, where a soldier can stand. The copy is not cited, as the entry already has five sources.

units.name: Submarine

tier.basis: Built at the Soviet Submarine Pen with no other tech building (infobox; StrategyWiki); the infobox gives tier 1, and the manual's Sub Pen entry names it among what the Pen builds.

cost_band.basis: The list price equals the Soviet Heavy Tank's, a little above the main-battle-tank anchor, so medium.

mobility.notes: Its water speed is a little over four fifths of the Rifle Infantry's pace (see uncertain). Among ships it keeps pace with the Destroyer, is slower than the Gunboat, and it is faster than the Missile Submarine and the Cruiser. It travels under water and comes up only to fire. The word list gives the naval mobility types no default handling, so steer is proposed: a submarine turns in arcs while under way. The sprite turning on the spot, as RTS models do, does not decide it.

body.notes: A teardrop-hulled attack submarine. Large, as the size list puts submarines; no page gives its footprint.

armour.notes: Step 1 decided: the infobox armour type Light maps to light; the manual's Armor word Medium is a grade, not the game's type. Its health is under a third of the Destroyer's. Like every ship it slows down at half health or less and is repaired by docking at a Sub Pen (game-wide).

sensors.notes: The infobox sight is one and a half times the Rifle Infantry's, on the edge, so medium. It finds other submerged submarines (Stealth page; the Submarine Pen's production list says so too). Like every ship it also makes a cloaked enemy right beside it shimmer into view, which is game-wide and gives no trait.

armament.name: Torpedoes
armament.summary: Torpedoes with an armour-piercing warhead, fired only after the sub surfaces and only while it is stopped. They run through water alone: the code allows them against ships, buildings that sit in the water (the Naval Yard and the Sub Pen) and bridges, and only when open water lies all the way to the target with no friendly boat in between. Land targets and aircraft are out of reach. A long pause separates shots. Reach is three times the rifle's, past its own sight.

crew.notes: One player steers and fires. The source has no seats and names no crew.

abilities.name: Cloaked when not attacking (submerged)
abilities.summary: It stays under water, unseen by the enemy, whenever it is not attacking, and moves freely while under. It comes up to fire and is then open to anything nearby that can hit it; it dives again only once its torpedoes have reloaded and no target is in reach. Taking damage also brings it up, and at low health it often fails to dive. While it is under, no enemy can target it, but detectors (the Destroyer, the Gunboat and other subs) and the Allied Sonar Pulse bring it into view.

on_death.notes: No page read shows survivors, and the game code gives ships no survivor logic, so the 3C default for a crewed machine applies.

strengths.why: Silent and unseen while under water, and no enemy can fire on it there, so it chooses when to surface and strike.
Its torpedoes reach three times the rifle's range, past its own sight, so it attacks ships from afar (manual).
Its armour-piercing torpedoes hit ships hard: StrategyWiki rates it strong against ships, and the wiki calls them deadly to most vessels.
It spots other hidden submarines near it (Stealth page).

weaknesses.why: Torpedoes run only through water: it cannot attack anything on land or in the air, so it needs other units to defend it from those.
It must surface to fire, which gives away where it is (manual), and it stays up until its tubes reload.
Light armour and modest health: once depth charges find it, it is out of the fight quickly (manual).

countered_by.why: Destroyers, and Gunboats in numbers, find submerged subs, and their depth charges fire at any sub they detect (manual).
The manual says a Destroyer that detects a sub takes it out of the fight rapidly with its twin depth-charge launchers.
A Spy that gets into a Sub Pen earns the one-shot Sonar Pulse, which shows every enemy sub on the map for a short while (manual).
The Allied Spy is the unit that wins the Sonar Pulse by entering a Soviet Sub Pen.

counters.why: It strikes ships from hiding and from afar; ships without depth charges have no way to answer it (manual, StrategyWiki), and even a Gunboat, which has them, loses one against one.
The manual calls the Cruiser a favourite target of submarines: it has no sea-based defence and relies on Destroyers and Gunboats.

combos.why: With nothing that reaches land, subs need aircraft to support them, the wiki says.

units.memorable: Red Alert's Soviet attack sub: invisible under the waves until it surfaces to torpedo a ship, then exposed until it can dive again.
units.as_player: Research only (naval). As a player unit you would cruise unseen and pick your moment: every shot brings you up, and you stay visible until the tubes reload, so each attack is a commitment. You can hit only ships and targets on the water, and detector ships with depth charges are your hard counter.

sources.note: The ship firing checks: torpedoes only at ships, floating buildings and bridges, with open water to the target and no friendly boat in the way; a ship without a turret cannot fire while moving; depth charges serve only against submarines, and a ship weapon whose projectile lacks the anti-submarine flag cannot target them; a sub surfaces before it fires and cannot dive again while a sonar pulse holds it.

uncertain.note: Several details come from REDALERT/TECHNO.CPP of the same source release (read, not cited): an enemy that is fully hidden cannot be fired on; any damage brings a hidden unit up; at low health it starts and finishes diving only by chance; it will not dive while reloading or while a target is in reach. The Missile submarine page (Command & Conquer Wiki, read, not cited) agrees that subs come up when attacked.
That no enemy can fire on it while it is under rests on REDALERT/TECHNO.CPP (read, not cited); the cited pages say only that it is hidden and silent until it surfaces.
That it stays up until its tubes reload rests on REDALERT/TECHNO.CPP (read, not cited), which holds back the dive while the weapon reloads or a target is in reach.

REDALERT/HOUSE.CPP (read, not cited) shows the Sonar Pulse bringing up every Submarine and Missile Submarine at once and keeping them from diving for a fixed time; the manual says it lasts a few seconds. The Sonar pulse page of the Command & Conquer Wiki (read, not cited) repeats the manual.

Structures rest on VESSEL.CPP letting torpedoes be fired at buildings that float (the Naval Yard and Sub Pen) and at bridges, and on the Submarine page's line that the torpedoes are very effective against naval yards. The reference copy of Rules.ini (OpenRA's raclassic repository, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OpenRA/raclassic/master/ref/Rules.ini) gives the damage: both yards have light armour, against which the torpedoes' armour-piercing warhead does three quarters of its full damage. The same copy gives the torpedo projectile the anti-submarine flag as well as the underwater one, and VESSEL.CPP lets a ship fire at a Submarine or Missile Submarine only with a weapon whose projectile has that flag, so the torpedoes can also be fired at other submarines; naval covers them.
REDALERT/BULLET.CPP (read, not cited) moves a torpedo cell by cell through water and sets it off on the first unit in its path or where the water ends; projectile is also the family default.
The Submarine Pen (Red Alert 1) page (Command & Conquer Wiki, read, not cited) also lists the Submarine as detecting submerged units; the cited Stealth page says the same.
Large by the size list's submarine example. No page gives the hull's footprint, so the example cannot be checked against a measurement.

Banded from a reading of EA's released code that no play test or community source confirms. Vehicles and ships share one movement routine, which halves the top speed of a unit carrying a flag, and it makes that check on ships too. In a ship, the byte it reads (VESSEL.H and UNIT.H) never holds the no-flag value, so every ship sails at half its rated speed. That leaves the Submarine at a little over four fifths of the Rifle Infantry's pace, which is slow: level with the Destroyer, and ahead of both the Missile Submarine and the Cruiser. If ships in fact sail at full rate, it would be well over one and a half times the rifleman's pace (fast).

The comparisons with other ships (speed here, health in armour.notes) come from the infoboxes of the Destroyer (Red Alert 1), Gunboat (Red Alert 1), Cruiser and Missile submarine pages on the Command & Conquer Wiki, read but not cited.

The manual's paragraph names ships, which match none of the three anti roles (registry notes), and the torpedoes hit nothing an anti role covers, so step 4 gives nothing and step 5 gives assault: slow, not fast (at the full-rate reading it would be fast and step 5 would give raider).

That one Gunboat loses to it while several win (countered_by/0) rests on the Gunboat (Red Alert 1) page of the Command & Conquer Wiki (https://cnc.fandom.com/wiki/Gunboat_(Red_Alert_1)), read but not cited.

fit_notes.note: A hidden torpedo boat that hunts ships comes out as frontline assault by step 5, because ships are no anti role's target. The role does not describe it.
The naval mobility types have no default handling, and the Handling tie-break starts from the default, so the proposal has no rule to follow.

The sub dives and surfaces by itself, with no key, and naval-submerged already says it moves under water and surfaces to act. The burrow trait is a key, and its class list leaves out naval, so it is not coded; the passive ability carries the burrow pattern.
